body:
In Brief
Posted:
3:47 PM PDT · October 28, 2026

Image Credits:Apple

		
							
											
									
					
	

Apple has officially entered the touchscreen MacBook Pro era, and apparently, it wants to drain your wallet while it’s at it.
The new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899, which is already a hefty price tag in this economy. But if you want the absolute top-of-the-line model with every possible upgrade, prepare to cough up around $14,549. 
As MacRumors first reported, Apple’s configurator prices the fully loaded 14-inch model at $14,249 and the 16-inch version at $14,549. Both come equipped with Apple’s top-tier M5 Max chip, featuring an 18-core CPU and 40-core GPU.
You can blame the ongoing memory shortage and AI’s seemingly endless appetite for hardware for some of the pricing pressure. Moving to a 4TB SSD costs an additional $1,000, while upgrading to 8TB adds $3,000. Want the new 16TB option? That’ll set you back another $7,000. 
Another $2,000 gets you 128GB of memory, while nano-texture glass adds $150.
For some perspective, the previous 16-inch MacBook Pro topped out at $10,149. The new model raises that ceiling by a whopping $4,400.
Absurd prices aside, the launch marks a significant shift for Apple, nearly a decade after it first experimented with the Touch Bar. The company eventually abandoned that feature, but now it’s ready to embrace a touchscreen MacBook Pro.
Preorders open October 30, with availability beginning November 6.

Ahead of the holiday season, A
body:
In Brief
Posted:
6:00 AM PDT · October 29, 2026

Image Credits:Getty Images

		
							
											
									
					
	

Ahead of the holiday season, Amazon has added more than 100 new shopping-related capabilities to Alexa, including managing subscriptions and lists, updating delivery instructions, solving payment issues, and answering questions about Prime subscriptions.
The update allows you to use Alexa to create lists, register them, see what’s on them, and add or edit items. You can also manage subscriptions with the AI bot — for example, you could ask it to change deliveries for an item to every three months instead of every month — and edit delivery instructions, such as change an address or add drop-off details.
Users also can now ask Alexa about their Prime or Audible subscriptions, and ask it questions about billing or payment issues.
Amazon has launched various AI-centric shopping features this year, including a shopping assistant and a way to notify users about new products and offers.
The company said that since the start of the year, the number of people using agentic features has grown 8x, and over the last 12 months, over 400 million consumers have used Alexa for shopping.

A top executive of a Singapore AI cl
body:
In Brief
Posted:
9:42 AM PDT · October 29, 2026

Image Credits:Nvidia

		
							
											
									
					
	

A top executive of a Singapore AI cloud firm that was accused of illegally selling Nvidia chips to China could also have been a Chinese spy, anonymous sources told the New York Times.
The executive, Alice Huang (or Huang Le), worked for Megaspeed and was photographed as one of multiple people hanging out with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during various business dinners in the Singapore region. U.S. intelligence agencies had been surveilling Alice Huang to learn more about her ties with China for about a year, the Times reports.
The concern, sources said, was that Alice Huang had grown so close to Jensen Huang that she could have been gathering information about Nvidia’s plans and the CEO’s efforts to convince the Trump administration to allow it to ship more advanced technology to China.
But an Nvidia spokesperson denied this, telling TechCrunch that the CEO’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was the same as with any other regional customer.
“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement. The company also said, “Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security.”
In 2025, the Times reported that the Commerce Department had investigated Megaspeed over concerns that it was helping Chinese companies sidestep AI chip export regulations by reselling restricted chips to them. Alice Huang was said to be a top executive for the firm at the time.

title: Microsoft just shared Azure’s actual revenue in dollars: $33.2 billion
description: Microsoft has never disclosed Azure’s quarterly revenue in dollars. It has typically only shared a growth percentage or described revenue dollar mile
body:
Microsoft has never disclosed Azure’s quarterly revenue in dollars. It has typically only shared a growth percentage or described revenue dollar milestones in vague ways. But on Wednesday, when it posted another record-breaking quarter, it reported that Azure brought in a healthy $33.2 billion in revenue for the July-September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier.
The disclosure lets investors line up Azure’s performance more directly against Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, whose parent companies already report cloud revenue in dollars every quarter. 
Alphabet, which also reported earnings on Wednesday, said Google Cloud brought in $30.7 billion in the same quarter, putting Azure slightly ahead. But Google Cloud, which also includes Google’s Workspace subscriptions, roughly doubled its revenue from a year earlier, growing about twice as fast as Azure, according to TechCrunch’s calculations.
Azure, where businesses rent computing power to run applications, SaaS, and to build and run AI models, is now Microsoft’s largest and fastest-growing product line by the company’s own figures. It accounted for roughly 36% of Microsoft’s $92.3 billion in quarterly revenue.
Azure’s revenue was also about $850 million more than the $32.3 billion analysts expected. Azure’s 48% growth rate also topped the 44% to 45% that Microsoft CFO Amy Hood forecast on the company’s July earnings call.
Azure sits inside Agents and Infra, one of two new business segments Microsoft introduced this quarter. Microsoft previously reported three segments, Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. The new Agents and Infra segment, which groups Azure with Microsoft 365’s cloud business, brought in $76.8 billion, up 25% from a year earlier.
Amazon reports its earnings on Thursday. Analysts also expect its cloud, Amazon Web Services, to grow. It’s been the largest cloud since the beginning of time and no one expects Microsoft to best it right now. But with all of them reporting actual dollars, the race is on.

title: Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI
description: Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended Septemb
body:
Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday. That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers. 
(Microsoft’s financial year begins in July, making the quarter ended September 30, 2026 the first quarter of its fiscal 2027.)
For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion. At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.
Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June. That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.   
It’s not clear how much of Microsoft’s revenue from OpenAI came from revenue-sharing payments or Azure cloud computing services. TechCrunch has reached out for more information. In November 2025, TechCrunch reported, citing leaked documents, that Microsoft had received $865.8 million in net revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI during the first nine months of that year.
OpenAI reportedly shares 20% of its revenue with Microsoft as part of a previous deal in which the software giant invested more than $13 billion in the AI startup. (Neither the AI lab nor Microsoft have publicly confirmed this percentage.) As part of an April 2026 agreement, OpenAI is on the hook to continue sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030, subject to a cap, even as OpenAI is allowed to work with competing cloud providers. 
The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers. In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement. 
Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September. That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization. Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

title: Deepgram acquires Pipecat-maker Daily to bolster its voice AI infrastructure
description: The voice AI sector is hot, and top players are trying to consolidate their position as more business models come to the fore through partnerships an
body:
The voice AI sector is hot, and top players are trying to consolidate their position as more business models come to the fore through partnerships and acquisitions. Deepgram is the latest to make such moves: The company said on Thursday that it is acquiring Daily, the maker and maintainer of one of the most popular open source voice AI infrastructures, Pipecat.
The companies didn’t disclose the deal amount but said that they will keep Pipecat open source.
For the uninitiated, Pipecat is a framework that manages voice and video streams along with other pieces in the pipeline, like speech-to-text (STT), large language models (LLMs), and text-to-speech (TTS) models while reducing latency. Its maker, Daily, provides hosted infrastructure for voice and video calls of any kind.
With Pipecat, Deepgram will likely gain a deeper understanding of real-time voice and video infrastructure. 
Daily has raised over $62 million in funding to date from investors such as Tiger Global, Highfield Capital, Nat Friedman, Lachy Groom, and Kevin Weil, according to PitchBook data. Earlier this year, Deepgram reached unicorn status with a $130 million Series C round. Incidentally, both companies were in the same Y Combinator batch in 2016.
Kwindla Kramer, Daily’s co-founder, said around the time when GPT-4 came out, the company started experimenting with AI-to-human communication over voice and text, which eventually resulted in the Pipecat framework. He noted that while there has been a lot of acquisition interest, he favored Deepgram’s CEO Scott Stephenson’s commitment to keeping Pipecat open source forever, and the engineering culture of both organizations matched, giving Daily’s team the freedom to work on different parts of the stack within a bigger organization.
“Scott was super committed to Pipecat being open source and vendor-neutral forever. I think there is both a personal commitment and commercial driver there. If you sit in the middle of an ecosystem that’s growing very fast, and have many parts of that ecosystem that are genuinely the best from your company, then everything being as open as possible is like a commercial advantage,” Kramer told TechCrunch.
Stephenson said that Deepgram has been wanting to work in open source for a long time, and the company realized that an orchestration framework for agents was a potential area, which drove the decision to partner with Daily.
“We want to open up the ecosystem so everybody can build voice agents. It’s great if you’re using Deepgram models, but I want you to be using the best models for your use case. And if Deepgram notices that we have some ground to catch up on in a certain area for our own models and products, that’s great. We want you to use partners, and then we’ll also work on becoming better in those areas,” he said.
Stephenson said the acquisition lets developers build agents with expressivity and end-to-end speech systems by plugging in different models and a context bus that connects all parts.
For Deepgram, the deal also lets it explore areas beyond voice through Pipecat, as the framework caters to real-time communication in different formats.
“We never thought about Pipecat as a voice toolkit. We thought about it as the toolkit we needed to build this new kind of AI-native software. Because of where we came from, we just always assumed real-time,” Kramer said.
Deepgram is also launching Real-Time Context Standard (RCS), an open protocol for voice agents that it co-developed with the Pipecat team. The protocol defines metadata like context from the audio, like a whisper, instructions for a language model on how it can use those signals, and guidance on how the response should sound.
Voice AI has seen a lot of investment from both the model and the infrastructure sides. Model makers like ElevenLabs, Gradium, and Fish Audio have raised millions of dollars. On the other hand, infrastructure companies like LiveKit and Vapi have raised multimillion-dollar funding rounds this year.

title: Google expands AI Search ads globally as core ad growth slows
description: Google is bringing ads in its AI-powered Search experiences to international markets, betting that generative AI can open up new revenue opportunitie
body:
Google is bringing ads in its AI-powered Search experiences to international markets, betting that generative AI can open up new revenue opportunities even as growth in its core search advertising business slows.
The announcement came Wednesday during Alphabet’s third-quarter earnings call, as the company reported $127.6 billion in revenue, up 25% year over year. But Search advertising growth continued to decelerate, and Alphabet shares fell 8% following the results.
Google Search revenue grew 12% year over year in the third quarter, down from 17% growth in the second quarter and 19% in the first quarter. The slowdown puts added pressure on Google to turn its expanding AI features into a meaningful source of advertising revenue.
“We are now scaling high-quality ads within AI overviews in AI mode to more users and queries,” Philipp Schindler, Google’s chief business officer, said during the call with investors. “This includes taking our monetization footprint global for the first time. Today, we’re announcing the expansion of ads in AI mode into international markets alongside multi-turn ads and AI mode in the U.S.”
Google says early results suggest the formats are working. Click-through rates for sponsored product listings in AI Mode are already comparable to those for organic listings, according to Schindler. The company’s user research also indicates that people find the ads relevant.
The move builds on Google’s May announcement of new Gemini-powered ad formats, including conversational discovery ads that respond to users’ questions and sponsored recommendations integrated into AI-generated answers. 
Google CEO Sundar Pichai also said that Search queries grew at their fastest year-over-year rate in five years, though he did not disclose the exact growth rate. He credited AI features with changing how people use Search, including prompting longer and more complex queries.
Queries in AI Mode are three times longer on average than traditional searches, Pichai said, while one in five AI Mode searches globally involves voice, images, or documents. Google has also surpassed 50 billion visual searches per month.
“[Search] is bringing the benefits of AI to more people than any other product in the world,” Pichai told investors. “People are using our AI features more, searching in entirely new ways. Their queries are longer, personalized, and multimodal.”
Alphabet’s Google Services division, which includes Search, generated $96.3 billion in revenue, up 11% year over year. Google Cloud revenue surged 103% to $30.7 billion.
The results follow a busy quarter for Google, including the release of Gemini 4 Argon, the growth of the Gemini app to 1 billion monthly users, and the launch of its Pixel 11 lineup.

title: Upwind raises $400M after walking away from Datadog acquisition offer
description: Upwind, a San Francisco startup that uses AI to secure cloud infrastructure, has raised a $400 million Series C round at a $3.8 billion valuation led
body:
Upwind, a San Francisco startup that uses AI to secure cloud infrastructure, has raised a $400 million Series C round at a $3.8 billion valuation led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from existing backers including Greylock Partners and Craft Ventures.
The round comes nine months after Upwind closed its previous $250 million financing at a $1.5 billion valuation.
The fresh funding, which has been in the works for months, nearly fell apart after Datadog attempted to buy the company, according to a person familiar with Upwind. Datadog is a publicly traded company that sells tools for monitoring how software runs, known as observability. It didn’t offer a premium above the $3.8 billion valuation set by venture capital investors, the person said, so Upwind decided to stay independent.
Four-year-old Upwind has grown rapidly amid rising AI-driven cybersecurity threats. The startup has been adding $20 million to $30 million in annualized recurring revenue (ARR) each quarter and is projected to end the year at roughly $90 million, according to a person familiar with Upwind’s financials. That means that VCs and Datadog valued the startup at more than 40 times its forecast ARR, a common yardstick for pricing software companies. The high multiple is also well below the 80x ARR fetched by Cyera, another fast-growing cybersecurity startup, according to TechCrunch reporting from earlier this year.
Cybersecurity is poised to be the third big wave of AI software that companies will pay for after AI coding tools and customer support, Theory Ventures general partner Tomasz Tunguz recently wrote in his widely read blog.
By walking away from an acquisition offer, Upwind clearly believes that the company will ultimately be worth more than the $3.8 billion that Datadog was ready to pay for it. However, given how few cybersecurity companies have gone public in recent years, an eventual sale remains the most likely outcome for the startup.
Upwind continues to draw acquisition interest, according to a person familiar with the company.
The startup was founded by Amiram Shachar, who sold his previous company, the cloud spend management startup Spot.io, to NetApp for $450 million. Upwind calls its approach to thwarting threats “runtime” security, which means it alerts and remedies attacks and vulnerabilities in active services in real time.
TechCrunch has reached out to both Upwind and Datadog for comment.

title: Bluesky blocks links to leaked DHS employee data as government seeks takedowns
description: Following a sizable leak of personnel data about employees who work for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, social network Bluesky is now block
body:
Following a sizable leak of personnel data about employees who work for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, social network Bluesky is now blocking its users from accessing a nonprofit’s website that hosts the leaked dataset.
Users reported that the links to nonprofit transparency collective DDoSecrets were marked as “malicious” soon after TechCrunch and other media outlets broke the news that Homeland Security had been hacked.
A screenshot showing Bluesky blocking links to DDoSecretsImage Credits:TechCrunch
TechCrunch reported on Wednesday that a hacker obtained over 40,000 user account records from Homeland Security’s login system, including the names and contact information, such as work-issued phone numbers and email addresses, of employees and agents working for its various agencies like Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The data included information that was similar to that on an employee’s business card. DDoSecrets, which publishes leaked datasets in the public interest, also made the hacked data publicly available. Researchers who are investigating abuses by the Trump administration say that the data will be invaluable for seeking records from the government under public records laws.
A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch on Wednesday that it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.” 
In a statement, Bluesky chief operating officer Rose Wang told TechCrunch: “Our Community Guidelines protect people’s safety and privacy by prohibiting the unauthorized sharing of personal information and other content that could pose safety risks. Because the files include the email addresses and phone numbers of individuals, shared without their authorization, we are blocking links to the dataset.”
“When deciding between blocking a link and removing individual posts, we chose to block the links to avoid limiting public discussion or restricting broader access to reporting and commentary,” said Wang.
In a post on Bluesky, Wang said that the company plans to change the wording on the block message. “We should have changed the wording last night. Changes incoming shortly,” said Wang.
DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best told TechCrunch that while Bluesky’s terms of service prohibit sharing home addresses and personal contact information, Best said that neither of these is in the leaked dataset.
“The data contains professional contact information for government employees at a time when the public interest in that exact information has never been higher. By requiring the public to provide it for [Freedom of Information Act] requests, the government has made that exact information a crucial piece of the transparency channels they want the public to engage in,” said Best.
Homeland Security sends takedown notices
Best told TechCrunch that a website hosting a searchable copy of the stolen data was taken down by its domain registrar, effectively knocking the website offline for now.
A search site, dubbed Icepick, made by journalist maia arson crimew no longer loads as of Thursday morning. An internet record associated with the domain says it has been placed on “serverHold,” which generally means that the domain registrar locked or closed the domain for some reason.
Homeland Security filed a takedown notice via a security vendor called ZeroFox, which has authority to act on the department’s behalf until 2028 to seek the removal of data from the internet. TechCrunch has seen a copy of the takedown notice for the search site, which asks that the domain registrar “stop serving the personal contact and location data of individuals who did not consent to its publication.” 
CentralNic, which hosts the domain name, did not respond to a request for comment from TechCrunch about the takedown or whether it was instructed to do so by a government demand. ZeroFox also did not respond to a request for comment. 
The Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up regarding the takedown notice affecting Icepick’s website.
Crimew also made a locally hosted version of the data, allowing anyone to access it on their own computer. 
Updated with comment from Bluesky.

title: Microsoft hits 10 quarters of record-breaking revenue in a row
description: Whatever the future of AI might be, the current situation is still very good for Microsoft. The tech giant reported yet another quarterly revenue rec
body:
Whatever the future of AI might be, the current situation is still very good for Microsoft. The tech giant reported yet another quarterly revenue record on Wednesday: $92.3 billion, a 19% increase over the year-ago quarter.
Microsoft has now reported record-breaking revenue for 10 quarters in a row.
Image Credits:TechCrunch
This is profitable revenue, too. Microsoft reported that net income reached $36.6 billion, an increase of 32% on a GAAP basis, over the year-ago quarter.
The record-breaking income was largely driven on the strength of Microsoft Cloud, which reached $63.9 billion in revenue this quarter, an increase of 30% over the year-ago quarter, Microsoft said.
Microsoft has reorganized its business reporting into two basic segments: 1) Agents and Infra and 2) Devices and Consumer. On the flip side, revenue in Devices and Consumer was $15.5 billion, decreased of 3%, with Windows OEM and devices revenue falling 22% from the year-ago quarter.
True, not all of Microsoft’s healthy cloud revenue can be attributed to AI. Microsoft 365 accounted for nearly $28 billion. But Azure brought in the most, at $33.2 billion. And again, not all of that is necessarily AI-related. Enterprises run all sorts of the traditional software and SaaS applications on Azure.
Still, a good chunk of the revenue was from AI, because Microsoft also reported $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI. Despite branching out to AWS, Oracle, and others, OpenAI still runs a lot of its services on Microsoft’s cloud. (Anthropic runs on Azure as well.) Microsoft also said its “commercial remaining performance obligation increased 73% to $677 billion.” That represents future revenue committed under existing contracts of the AI labs.
But, like all the big cloud providers, Microsoft is also spending big to prepare to deliver on those commitments. Capital expenditures topped $45.2 billion, another all-time quarterly record.

title: Agent identity startup Mintive lands Cowboy Ventures, Coatue, angels Jeff Dean, Andrej Karpathy
description: Here’s another early-stage, agent-management startup to watch because of the backgrounds of the founders and the sheer number of big names it has alr
body:
Here’s another early-stage, agent-management startup to watch because of the backgrounds of the founders and the sheer number of big names it has already attracted as investors: Mintive.
Mintive has raised $11 million total, including a newly announced $7 million seed led by Cowboy Ventures. Additional investors include Coatue, Operator Collective, and Hustle Fund; angels include Okta co-founder Frederic Kerrest, Discovery Loop co-founder and former Google Chief Scientist Jeff Dean, and OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy, among others.
Mintive was founded by Jiquan Ngiam (pictured above, far right) and Vijay Vasudevan (pictured above far left). Ngiam, Mintive’s CEO, was the founding engineer of Coursera (employee No. 1, hired by Andrew Ng). Ngiam later worked on neural networks at Google Brain. Vasudevan, the company’s CTO, is best known as one of the co-creators of TensorFlow while he was at Google Brain. That was the OG AI training platform that predated PyTorch.
Mintive is joining a crowded field of products that promise to govern, provision, and offer identity management to enterprise AI agents. Its platform includes an MCP gateway that allows IT professionals to authorize what the cloud services agents may access and what actions they can perform on them. It also offers an LLM gateway that routes to different models and can cap costs; handles agent identities and authorizations that may differ from the employees that they serve; and an agent monitor that tracks all agents across the company. The company also allows enterprises to create agents that proactively perform long-running tasks.
Still, it’s hard to imagine a field with more competition. Agent management systems are offered by Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, plus as point products galore (from companies as diverse as LangChain, New Relic, and Rippling, to name a few). Then there are countless startups working on the idea (40+ from Y Combinator alone).
So, what’s Mintive’s secret sauce? Given the founders’ long history in building AI for enterprises, they have designed their system to be especially easy to use, Ngiam says. Set-up amounts to clicking a few buttons, the startup promises.
“I think what our customers look at and they are a bit shocked at, is how quick it is and easy to deploy,” Ngiam tells TechCrunch. “We have really thought through all the ways this can be done, all the access control, permissioning layer, to make it so easy for them to deploy it, that all the complexities are hidden away. You don’t think about sandboxes, you don’t think about harnesses, you don’t think about memory because we manage that for you.”
That pitch has won over 50 enterprise customers so far, Mintive says, since the startup launched its product in February. These include Ro, Modern Treasury, the University of Michigan, Coursera, Apax, and Stability AI.
But it was the founders’ industry experience that won over Cowboy Ventures managing partner Aileen Lee. 
“AI is going to be able to power incredible things, but we need more infrastructure that’s going to give us governance and visibility and control,” Lee told TechCrunch.
Lee also says she particularly respects that Ngiam has been careful by only raising $11 million. This compares to other agentic-building startups raising vast amounts at unicorn valuations. As just one example: Prime Intellect raised $130 million for its Series A at $1 billion valuation.
“I feel really lucky to have won the chance to work with him,” said Lee. “He is a grown-up and so he was not a person chasing a ‘vanity’ round.”
Lee added: “I think a lot of companies are being set up for failure by chasing round size, rather than, ‘how much do I need to actually really move the needle for the company?’ And so, yes, in a time when people are raising unprecedented amounts of money, we’re just kind of doing it the brick by brick, old-fashioned way.”

title: Ex-Palantir execs launch Dream with $17M from a16z to build AI world models for construction
description: Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Elder led product design
body:
Andy Elder and Arjun Mathur were Stanford roommates who both studied computer science before spending a decade at Palantir. Elder led product design for a team of 800 people building software for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, while Mathur served as a senior vice president in the company’s commercial practice. When the friends decided to build a startup early last year, there was no question they would do it together.
Despite having no direct background in architecture, Elder and Mathur were troubled by a growing problem: Fewer buildings are constructed in the U.S. today than a few decades ago, as development costs have surged.
“We’ve gone from dial-up internet to superintelligent AI, but our ability to build the physical world around us has actually decreased,” Mathur told TechCrunch.
Believing AI can boost productivity across the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, they set out to build Dream, a startup developing built world models that automate building design and engineering. Dream has emerged from stealth with $17 million in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, alongside other backers, including SV Angel, XYZ, and Zigg Capital. The startup aims to replace cumbersome, outdated AEC tools like Autodesk’s AutoCAD and Revit.
If you sit next to an architect or a structural engineer, you’ll notice that they are still “drawing” every piece of their designs part by part on legacy software, Mathur said. “AI really plays no role in that equation.”
While a standard LLM like ChatGPT can generate an image of a building, the result won’t be structurally sound. Dream, by contrast, is grounded in real physics and construction standards. Just as LLMs learn from text, Dream’s world model is trained on more than 100 million square feet of building data gathered from permit archives across the United States.
“Our model actually understands what’s within those walls. What materials are used, what the beams are made of, and how much weight they can support,” Elder said.
The startup calls its approach “structural cognition” because its model generates structurally precise designs that account for internal building elements like plumbing and HVAC.
Dream has already begun selling its product to AEC professionals and developers, who use the model to conceptualize building designs and estimate overall costs, according to the founders. The platform is already deployed across 10 active projects in Texas and California.
While Dream isn’t the only company attempting to update AEC software with AI — other startups working on this include Motif, Snaptrude, and Arcol — Elder and Mathur claim that they are the only ones that developed a world model that instantly designs whole buildings.
Kimberly Tan, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that while the firm first invested in Dream over a year ago, when the startup model was just an idea, she has been extremely impressed with their progress. “I have not seen anybody take the technical approach,” she said. “They’re doing everything based on their own models.”

title: Wabi, the AI agent that builds mini apps, now valued at $1.25B after latest round
description: The race to build the winning AI assistant is on, and investors are spreading out their bets. On Thursday, another AI app, Wabi, now describing itsel
body:
The race to build the winning AI assistant is on, and investors are spreading out their bets. On Thursday, another AI app, Wabi, now describing itself as a “personal agent,” said it has raised $55 million at a $1.25 billion valuation.
Founded by Eugenia Kuyda, who previously founded the AI companion startup Replika, Wabi originally focused on allowing anyone to build apps using prompts. Last month, however, the startup announced a pivot of sorts to become an AI messenger. 
The idea now is that the new Wabi — or Wabi 2.0, as it was called — could build the interfaces you need to get things done as part of its role as your personal AI agent.
The company suggests Wabi could be used to build mini apps for things like meal planning, tracking local restaurants, planning date nights, creating fitness plans, designing specialized trivia games, and more.
Image Credits:Wabi
The additional funding indicates that Wabi’s investors agree that its new agentic angle has some potential, especially given the market around AI agents is hot right now, with viral AI agent Instinct pulling in another billion at a $10 billion valuation in September. 
Even Tolan, which makes a cute, Muppet-like AI companion to help people navigate life, just raised $30 million.
“Eugenia has a unique sense for where AI is headed and a track record of great taste in building it,” said Alex Lim, general partner at IVP, which led the new round, in a statement. “She has a clear vision for how people will interact with AI, one that goes far beyond the text box or command line. Wabi is the expression of that vision, and we’re thrilled to support her.”
Other participants in the round included Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Forerunner, Amazon Alexa Fund, and angel investors like Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, former Yahoo! head Marissa Mayer, former Twitter CEO Dick Costolo, and one half of The Chainsmokers, Alex Pall.

title: Mistral releases weights for its trillion-parameter AI model, targeting cybersecurity
description: French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and gov
body:
French AI company Mistral has released the weights for its trillion-parameter open source AI model Mistral Large 4 (ML4), allowing businesses and governments to download and deploy the system themselves. Nicknamed “Le Chonk,” the model was first introduced earlier this month.  
The release comes as competition between open-weight AI developers like Mistral and closed-model providers like OpenAI and Anthropic heats up, with the former arguing that businesses and governments shouldn’t have to rely on outside AI companies for access to advanced capabilities. That argument may hold more weight in cybersecurity, where organizations want more control over their data and systems. 
Or, as Mistral’s CEO, Arthur Mensch, explained, AI should “be a tool for empowerment, not dominance.” With Chonk, Mistral doubles down on that position, arguing that it’s able to achieve “state-of-the-art performance” at a “fraction of the compute and capital committed by closed labs.”
The release of the model’s weights — the numerical training that animates the system — ensures that other companies and government agencies will now be able to deploy ML4 for their own purposes.
Mistral says that its model is comparable in terms of performance with a Chinese open-weight competitor, GLM-5.3, which was previously considered one of the best open-weight models in the world — particularly when it comes to cyber work. However, Mistral’s model uses 47 percent fewer tokens per task, making it significantly more economical than GLM-5.3.
The company also claims that the model outranks all other open models when it comes to agentic coding tasks on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index, an AI benchmarking site. 
“Amid growing cyber threats, ML4 brings state-of-the-art sovereign cyber defense capabilities to enterprises and governments globally,” the company said Thursday. “Enterprise and public sector institutions can now download, deploy, and own frontier AI to detect, analyze, and respond to threats across code and IT infrastructure.”
The weights for ML4 are being made available on Hugging Face and via its API.
Pierre Stock, Vice President of Science at Mistral, told TechCrunch that the release of the model’s weights meant that organizations will have more control over how they use AI to defend themselves. 
“Concretely, it means that, for instance, as a business company or as a government, you’re able to have access to frontier intelligence to defend yourselves against cyberattacks. Access that can’t be cut off by definition because the model is open-weighted,” he said.
Stock added that the model could be used to “identify, coordinate, and respond in real time to major security incidents, and that the open sourcing means that companies can deploy this model on-prem in their own ecosystem. 
While advances in AI cybersecurity are helping security professionals to find bugs at a much higher rate than before, Stock continued, he believes it’s important for companies to “provide [this same] capability to everyone…as soon as possible to ramp up and to strengthen the ecosystem,” given that “some malicious actors might try to actually leverage their own technology to attack.”
Separately, Stock addressed concerns about recent incidents involving rogue AI agents, acknowledging the risks but cautioning against overreacting. 
“We don’t want to fearmonger people. We think it’s a problem that is solvable. It’s a hard problem to have good security,” he said.

title: Who will you learn from in 6 days at TechCrunch Founder Summit? Meet the founders and investors taking the stages
description: There are plenty of places to find startup advice. TechCrunch Founder Summit is about hearing what happened when people actually put that advice to t
body:
There are plenty of places to find startup advice. TechCrunch Founder Summit is about hearing what happened when people actually put that advice to the test.
Six days from now, TechCrunch Founder Summit, presented by Fidelity Private Shares, brings experienced founders, investors, and operators to Boston to share the decisions, mistakes, pivots, and lessons that shaped their companies. 
Register now to save up to $100, get a second ticket free when you buy one, or save up to 30% on group ticket bundles. Don’t miss these deals before the event starts on November 4.
Who and what are on the agenda
Explore the full Founder Summit agenda to discover the breakout and roundtable sessions and speakers bringing actionable insights, hard-earned lessons, and practical advice to help you scale your startup.
Image Credits:Halo Creative / Flickr (opens in a new window)
From Boston startup to public company
Few stories capture the potential of the Boston startup ecosystem better than Toast.
Steve Fredette, president, co-founder, and director of Toast, will talk about what it takes to keep reinventing a company even after the original idea works.
Scaling creates a new set of questions: How do you keep innovating? How do you stay close to the customers who got you there? And how do you evolve as technology and expectations change around you?
For founders trying to move from early traction toward meaningful scale, those are the questions that matter.
Know whether you’re actually ready to grow
Growth can be exciting. Premature growth can be expensive. Kent Bennett, partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, will explore how founders can recognize meaningful product-market fit before they scale.
Rudina Seseri, founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures, will take that conversation further by tackling when founders should accelerate and when hitting the brakes may be the smarter decision.
Together, those sessions give founders perspectives from both sides of the growth equation.
Build better teams, pitches, and companies
The agenda goes well beyond fundraising. Vineet Edupuganti of Cogent Security will explore how founders can build exceptional teams.
Dave Balter of True Ventures and Edisyl will focus on the pitch and why a founder’s goal isn’t to explain everything in one meeting. It’s to make someone want the next one.
Chase Garbarino of HqO will bring the conversation home with a look at what it takes to build and scale an ambitious company from Boston.
And Tina Tosukhowong of TDK Ventures will explore the signals investors look for when evaluating potential category leaders.
One day. A lot of experience in one room.
TechCrunch Founder Summit gives attendees access to people who have built companies, funded them, scaled them, hired through growth, sold into large enterprises, and made difficult calls when the right answer wasn’t obvious. Come with questions. Leave with perspectives you can actually use.
